sections.h2: Does Texas law set a real estate agent commission rate?
sections.html:
No. The Texas Real Estate Commission says it does not regulate the fees paid to any license holder, including buyer's agents, seller's agents, brokers, inspectors and appraisers, and that all fees come from your agreement with each professional. Anyone quoting a statewide percentage as a legal rate is describing a habit, not a rule.

TREC's consumer guide adds one instruction: read the fees in any representation or service agreement before you sign it. This page does not print a typical percentage, because no state page in the sources used here sets one.

sections.h2: What changed for buyer agreements and compensation in 2026?
sections.html:
Legislation from the 89th Texas Legislative Session changed the Real Estate License Act so that a license holder working with a residential buyer needs a written agreement before showing a home. If no home will be shown, the agreement is needed before the agent presents an offer for the buyer. TREC's article says the changes apply as of January 1, 2026.

The agreement has to state the amount or rate of the broker's compensation and how it will be figured. It also has to say in conspicuous language that broker compensation is not set by law and is fully negotiable. Commercial buyers and tenants fall outside the written-agreement rule.

  • Services the license holder will provide.
  • An end date for the agreement.
  • Whether it is exclusive or non-exclusive.
  • Whether the license holder represents the buyer.
  • The compensation amount or rate and how it is determined.

sections.h2: How long can a showing-only agreement last?
sections.html:
A non-representation, showing-only agreement can run no more than 14 days and must be non-exclusive, per TREC's article. A full representation agreement can narrow the services an agent offers, such as limiting them to showings, but cannot waive the minimum duties owed to a client.

For a Texas seller, the effect shows up in the offers you receive. A buyer's agent now arrives with a signed agreement that spells out how that agent expects to be paid, so the question of who covers that fee comes up early in negotiation instead of late.

sections.h2: What do agents owe me, and who handles complaints?
sections.html:
TREC's consumer guide says brokers and sales agents must put the client's interests above all others, acting as fiduciaries. The minimum services are telling the client any material information about the property or transaction, answering questions and presenting offers and counteroffers, and treating all parties honestly and fairly.

Agents must hand you the Information About Brokerage Services form the first time you discuss a specific property, along with the Consumer Protection Notice. If you think an agent is not treating you fairly, TREC accepts complaints and can act against a license holder who breaks the rules. TREC's license holder lookup shows whether a person holds an active license and any discipline.

sections.h2: Can an agent rebate part of the commission?
sections.html:
Yes. TREC's FAQ says a license holder may rebate part of the compensation to a party in the transaction without violating the license act or rules. If the rebate goes to a party the agent does not represent, the agent must first get the consent of the party the agent does represent, under Rule 535.147(d).

The same FAQ says an agent who advertises a rebate must follow Rule 535.155, and that a rebate may be limited by the buyer's lender. A listing broker also may not share compensation with someone who acts as a broker without a broker license, and the FAQ gives an attorney acting as buyer's agent as an example.

sections.h2: Do open houses and showings change who an agent works for?
sections.html:
They can. TREC's article on the 2026 changes says an agent hosting an open house who belongs to the listing broker's office only has to disclose that the agent represents the owner. A showing agent from another brokerage must hand over the Information About Brokerage Services form and sign a written agreement with a visiting buyer before the buyer starts viewing the home.

The article says a buyer who refuses to sign cannot be shown the property, and that license holders can face discipline for skipping the written agreement. For you as a Texas seller, that means a stranger at your open house may be asked to sign paperwork at the door, which is a legal requirement for the agent and not a sign of anything wrong with your listing.

The same article says two references to subagency were removed from the License Act. Subagency has not disappeared as a legal idea, so ask your broker or an attorney if a situation seems to involve it.

sections.h2: How does TREC treat commission sharing and trust accounts?
sections.html:
A listing broker may not share compensation with someone who acts as a broker without holding a broker license. TREC's FAQ applies this to an attorney who represents a buyer: the listing broker must still present the attorney's offer to the seller and tell the seller about the prohibition, and the seller and buyer may work out payment to a Texas attorney between themselves.

The same FAQ says a listing broker may agree to reduce the commission at a seller's request without breaking the splitting prohibition. Brokers who hold earnest money or other funds in a trust account must provide a monthly accounting when there has been activity, and must keep trust and escrow records for four years from the date the record is received or created.

  • Ask the broker where earnest money will be held.
  • Ask how a commission reduction would be written into the listing agreement.
  • Ask whether any buyer's attorney is involved, and how that attorney is paid.

sections.h2: What should I compare before I sign a listing agreement?
sections.html:
Put each offer on the same footing by comparing what reaches you after every cost. Commission is one line. Repairs, seller concessions, closing costs and any compensation you agree to pay toward the buyer's agent are others, and each is a contract term you can negotiate.

Terms TREC says belong in your agreement or contract
TermWhere TREC says it lives
Listing broker feeYour agreement with the broker, not set by TREC
Buyer agent compensationWritten buyer agreement, stated as amount or rate
Rebates to a partyRule 535.147(d) consent rule
Representation and dutiesInformation About Brokerage Services form

Ask your agent which of these appear in the paperwork you are asked to sign, and get each in writing.

sections.h2: What if I would rather sell without an agent commission?
sections.html:
You can list with a broker, sell yourself, or sell to a buyer who purchases directly, and each carries different costs and duties. A sale without a listing broker has no listing commission, but it also has no agent handling showings, paperwork or negotiation. TREC's contract forms are written for license holders, and TREC says complex or specialized situations may call for an attorney.

If the sale involves a buyer's agent, that agent's written agreement with the buyer states how the agent expects to be paid, and you can ask to see how it applies to your sale before you accept an offer.

faqs.q: Is real estate commission set by law in Texas?
faqs.a: No. TREC says it does not regulate fees paid to any license holder, and all fees are set by your agreement with each professional.

faqs.q: Must a Texas buyer sign something with an agent before touring a home?
faqs.a: Yes, for residential buyers. TREC says a written agreement is required before showing a home or, if none is shown, before presenting an offer.

faqs.q: Does the written buyer agreement say how the agent gets paid?
faqs.a: Yes. It must state the compensation amount or rate, how it is determined, and conspicuous wording that compensation is not set by law and is negotiable.

faqs.q: Can an agent give back part of a commission?
faqs.a: Yes. TREC's FAQ says a rebate to a party is permitted, and consent of the agent's own client is required first when the rebate goes to a party the agent does not represent.

faqs.q: Where do I complain about an agent?
faqs.a: File a complaint with TREC, which can act against a license holder who breaks the rules. Disputes over who gets earnest money are outside what TREC decides.
